What the official sources say

  • For separately assessed parcels, the limitation does not bar the action unless the adverse claimant (or predecessors) paid taxes on the land at least five consecutive years of the claimed occupancy. (Minn. Stat. 541.02 para. 2; source)
  • The tax-payment requirement does not apply to boundary-line actions established by adverse possession or to lands not assessed for taxation. (Minn. Stat. 541.02 para. 3; source)
  • A person who holds over after the redemption period on a mortgage foreclosure, execution sale or tax judgment sale, or holds over after lease termination or after tenancy-at-will notice to quit, may be removed by an eviction action. (Minn. Stat. 504B.285 subd. 1(a); source)

Minnesota Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Minnesota house?

Check the statute and talk to a Minnesota attorney about your facts.

Can someone take title to a Minnesota house just by living in it?

Only after a long wait, and the wait is written as a deadline on the owner's lawsuit. Minn. Stat. 541.02, titled "Recovery of real estate, 15 years," says no action to recover real estate or its possession can be maintained unless the plaintiff or the plaintiff's ancestor, predecessor or grantor was seized or possessed of the premises within 15 years before the action began.

Put plainly, an owner who has been out of possession for more than 15 years can lose the right to sue to get the property back. A person who moves into a vacant or unwatched house does not gain ownership on day one, a month later or a year later. The 15-year clock is the starting point for any adverse possession claim in Minnesota, and the statute does not list every other element a court will look at, so an owner facing a claim should speak with a Minnesota real estate attorney about the facts.

What does the property tax rule add to an adverse possession claim?

For a separately assessed parcel, the claimant must also have paid the property taxes. The second paragraph of section 541.02 says the 15-year limit is not a bar to the owner's action unless the person claiming title by adverse possession, or that person's ancestor, predecessor or grantor, or all of them together, paid taxes on the property for at least five consecutive years of the period they claim to have occupied it adversely.

That requirement has two stated exceptions in the third paragraph:

  • Actions about a boundary line that was established by adverse possession, including land between the government or platted line and the line established by that possession.
  • Land that is not assessed for taxation.

For an owner, the practical lesson is to keep an eye on the tax record. A parcel on which someone else has paid the tax for years is a warning sign, so check the county tax record now and then.

Does adverse possession work against Torrens or registered land?

No. Minn. Stat. 508.02 states that no title to registered land in derogation of the registered owner's title can be acquired by prescription or by adverse possession. The same section keeps the common law doctrine of practical location of boundaries for registered land.

The statute separates registered land from unregistered land. For unregistered land, the 15-year rule above is the one to study. For registered land, the county registrar of titles keeps a certificate of title, and the adverse possession route is closed. Ask the county recorder's office which kind of record covers your parcel.

When can an owner remove an occupant with an eviction case?

Eviction is the court process for people who stay on after their right to be there has ended. Minn. Stat. 504B.285, subdivision 1, lets the person entitled to the premises recover possession by eviction when someone holds over:

  • after a sale of the property on an execution or judgment;
  • after the redemption period on a mortgage foreclosure has ended, or after a contract to convey the property has been terminated;
  • after the redemption period on a real estate tax judgment sale has ended;
  • after the term of a lease has ended, contrary to its conditions, or after rent becomes due under the lease; or
  • as a tenant at will after the tenancy ended by notice to quit.

A person with no lease and no history with the owner does not fit neatly into those categories. In that case, the owner should ask a Minnesota attorney or the court's self-help staff which path applies. Do not change locks, remove belongings or cut off utilities before getting that advice.

Which notice periods protect tenants in a foreclosed or contract-for-deed home?

Residential tenants who lived in a property when it was foreclosed get extra time before the new owner can remove them. The main Minnesota rules for them are in subdivisions 1a and 1b of section 504B.285, and the table summarizes them.

Notice to vacate for tenants after foreclosure or contract termination
SituationNotice the new owner must giveProvision
Tenant under a lease that began after the mortgage but before redemption endedAt least 90 days' written notice, if the tenant pays rent and follows the leaseSubd. 1a(a)
Bona fide lease running more than 90 days past redemptionTenant stays to the end of the term, with 90 days' written notice; 90 days from redemption end if the new owner will live thereSubd. 1a(b)
Lease began after a contract for deed but before termination period endedAt least two months' written noticeSubd. 1b

A bona fide lease, as the statute defines it, is one where the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse or parent is not the tenant, the lease came from an arm's-length deal, and the rent is not substantially below fair market rent unless a government subsidy reduces it.

How does an eviction case move through a Minnesota court?

The owner files a complaint, the court issues a summons, and a hearing is set about one to two weeks out. Under Minn. Stat. 504B.321, the complaint states the full name and date of birth of the person being sued where known, describes the premises, and states the facts that justify recovering possession. The appearance date must fall between seven and 14 days after the summons is issued.

The complaint has to attach the lease if there is one, and a copy of any notice to vacate or notice to quit if the claim is a holdover under section 504B.285. A claim for unpaid rent needs a written notice first: the landlord must give the tenant at least 14 days, or longer where a local rule requires it, before filing.

An expedited hearing is available only for conduct that seriously endangers other residents or intentionally and seriously damages property, and the hearing then takes place five to seven days after the summons is issued. If a judge finds the request had no sufficient basis, the court can impose a civil penalty of up to $500. A case that fails the filing and service rules is dismissed and the record expunged, and eviction files are not open to the public until a final judgment is entered.

When does entering or staying in a house become a crime?

Minnesota's trespass statute makes several acts misdemeanors. Minn. Stat. 609.605, subdivision 1, covers a person who intentionally does any of these:

  • Trespasses on another person's premises and, without a claim of right, refuses to leave when the lawful possessor demands it.
  • Occupies or enters the dwelling or a locked or posted building of another without a claim of right or the consent of someone with the right to give it, except in an emergency.
  • Returns to the property, after being told to leave and not return, with intent to abuse, disturb, cause distress or threaten someone.
  • Returns within one year after being told to leave and not return, without a claim of right or consent.

The phrase "claim of right" is where disputes arise. A person who says they have a lease, a purchase contract or a family arrangement may be asserting a right, which is a question for the court. If a stranger has plainly broken in, call the police non-emergency line and get the report number for the file.

What if I need to sell a house that someone else occupies?

Resolve who has the right to be there first, then sell. A buyer or title company will want to know whether the house is vacant at closing, and an unresolved occupant can stall the sale. A properly handled eviction ends with a court judgment, which is the document that shows the occupant's right to stay is finished.

An occupied house usually sells for less and closes more slowly, so settle the occupancy first where you can. Whatever route you pick, keep copies of any lease, notices, court papers and photographs of the condition of the house. A Minnesota attorney can tell you which court procedure fits your facts.

More questions about Minnesota Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in Minnesota?

The statute sets a 15-year period. Minn. Stat. 541.02 bars an owner's action to recover real estate unless the owner or a predecessor possessed it within 15 years before suing, and for separately assessed parcels the claimant must also have paid taxes for at least five consecutive years.

Can squatters claim a house that is Torrens property?

No. Minn. Stat. 508.02 says no title to registered land can be acquired by prescription or adverse possession against the registered owner.

Can I just change the locks on a person living in my house?

Do not. Minnesota gives owners court procedures under chapter 504B for removing people who hold over, and entering or staying without a claim of right is a trespass offense that police handle. Ask an attorney or the court about the correct step before acting on your own.

How fast can a Minnesota eviction hearing be?

A regular hearing is set seven to 14 days after the summons is issued. An expedited hearing for serious endangerment or intentional serious property damage is set five to seven days after issuance, under Minn. Stat. 504B.321.

Does a squatter who pays the taxes get any better claim?

Paying the taxes is required on most parcels. For a separately assessed parcel, section 541.02 keeps the 15-year bar from applying against the owner unless the claimant paid taxes for at least five consecutive years of the claimed occupancy. Unassessed land and boundary-line claims are exceptions.

Minnesota Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Minnesota Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights sale
  • Turn the Minnesota Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Minnesota House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord must return the deposit with interest, or give a written statement of specific reasons for withholding, within three weeks after termination of tenancy (five days if tenant leaves due to legal condemnation), after receiving tenant's mailing address. (Minn. Stat. 504B.178 subd. 3; source)
  • A tenant may not withhold last month's rent on the ground that the deposit should serve as payment. (Minn. Stat. 504B.178 subd. 8; source)
  • Landlord entry requires a reasonable business purpose and good-faith effort at reasonable notice of not less than 24 hours, between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless agreed; showing the unit to a prospective buyer is a reasonable purpose; penalty up to $500 civil penalty per violation plus fees. (Minn. Stat. 504B.211 subds. 2, 3, 6; source)
  • Landlord covenants fitness, reasonable repair, compliance with health and safety laws, pest extermination and 68F heat Oct 1-Apr 30; covenants cannot be waived or modified. (Minn. Stat. 504B.161 subd. 1; source)
  • Tenant may not be evicted or have obligations increased/services decreased as a penalty for a complaint of a violation; landlord bears the burden within 90 days of the complaint. (Minn. Stat. 504B.441; source)
Selling in Minnesota?
We buy Minnesota houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What rights do Minnesota tenants keep when the landlord sells the building?

Minnesota's landlord and tenant rules sit in Chapter 504B, and several of them speak directly to a sale. The deposit has to move or be returned, the new owner steps into the old owner's deposit duties, and the landlord's right to bring buyers through the unit is limited by a notice rule.

What happens to the security deposit when a Minnesota rental is sold?

Subdivision 5 of Minn. Stat. 504B.178 gives the seller 60 days from the end of the landlord's interest, or less if the buyer has to account to the tenant sooner. Two choices exist. One is to hand the deposit, interest and lawful deductions included, to the buyer and then notify the tenant of the handoff along with the buyer's name and address. The other is to refund the tenant directly.

The buyer inherits the landlord's role for that money. A tenant who stays silent for 20 days after written notice of the amount locks the buyer's liability at the figure in the notice. That notice must include a stamped envelope addressed to the buyer and may go by mail or personal service. Deposits earn simple interest at one percent a year.

Mistakes cost money. A landlord who skips the transfer or refund owes a penalty equal to the withheld portion plus interest, in addition to the deposit itself. Bad faith adds punitive damages of up to $500 per deposit, and a missed deadline raises a presumption of bad faith that disappears only if the money is repaid within two weeks of a lawsuit being started.

How fast must a Minnesota landlord return a deposit at move-out?

A refund, or an itemized written explanation of what was kept, is due three weeks after the tenancy ends. If the tenant left because officials condemned the unit through no fault of the tenant, the deadline is five days. Both deadlines run from the moment the landlord has a forwarding address or delivery instructions.

Deductions are limited to what is reasonably needed for unpaid rent or agreed charges, or to return the unit to its move-in condition minus ordinary wear. If the tenant sues, the landlord has to prove every deduction.

  • Minn. Stat. 504B.182 requires the landlord to mention a move-in inspection option at the start of the tenancy or within 14 days.
  • A tenant who asks gets a move-out walkthrough, scheduled no sooner than five days before the lease ends.
  • A tenant may not skip the last month's rent and call the deposit payment. Doing so creates a rebuttable presumption and can bring a penalty and interest under subdivision 8.

Can a landlord show a Minnesota rental to a buyer?

Yes. Minn. Stat. 504B.211 names a buyer's visit as a reasonable business purpose. The landlord still has to try in good faith to give a day's notice, state a time or window, and stay within 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. unless the tenant agrees to other hours.

Real emergencies are carved out. A landlord who reasonably fears injury, property damage, a safety problem or an ordinance violation can enter at once. If nobody is home and no notice was given, a written note about the entry has to be left where the tenant will see it.

A landlord who breaks this rule may face a rent cut, up to full rescission of the lease, deposit return less lawful deductions, a civil penalty of as much as $500 for each violation, and the tenant's attorney fees. The same section treats a violation as a breach of the landlord covenants in 504B.161.

Which notice periods matter most in Minnesota landlord-tenant law?

Deadlines drive most disputes, and these are the ones that surface when an owner sells or a tenant moves out.

Minnesota landlord and tenant deadlines, with statute source
SituationPeriodSource
Deposit return after tenancy endsThree weeks (five days after condemnation)Minn. Stat. 504B.178
Deposit handling after a saleWithin 60 daysMinn. Stat. 504B.178
Tenant objection to transferred amount20 days after written noticeMinn. Stat. 504B.178
Landlord entry noticeAt least 24 hoursMinn. Stat. 504B.211
Wait after a nonpayment notice14 days, longer where local rules say soMinn. Stat. 504B.321
Ending a tenancy at willThe shorter of one rent interval or three monthsMinn. Stat. 504B.135
Ending a lease after the tenant diesTwo months written noticeMinn. Stat. 504B.265
Reminder about an automatic renewal clauseSent 15 to 30 days ahead of the tenant's cutoffMinn. Stat. 504B.145

What repairs and conditions must a Minnesota landlord provide?

Every residential lease carries covenants from Minn. Stat. 504B.161 that neither side can waive. The landlord promises fit premises and common areas, reasonable repair that includes pest control, sensible energy efficiency, and compliance with health, safety and rental licensing law. Heat must be at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in every place meant for living, kitchens and bathrooms too, from October 1 through April 30.

A landlord can ask a tenant to handle specific repairs only through a conspicuous written agreement supported by adequate consideration, and that agreement cannot waive these covenants or relieve the landlord of common area upkeep. Tenants facing an emergency can petition the court under Minn. Stat. 504B.381. Listed emergencies include a serious infestation, loss of water, heat or electricity, and a government condemnation.

Retaliation is off limits. Minn. Stat. 504B.441 forbids punishing a complaint with an eviction, a heavier obligation or fewer services, and when that happens inside 90 days the burden of proof sits with the landlord.

How does eviction work for unpaid rent in Minnesota?

A nonpayment case cannot start without a prior written notice under Minn. Stat. 504B.321. The notice must show the amount owed, itemize rent, late fees and other charges, name the person who can accept payment, and carry the legal aid and rental assistance language the statute prescribes. Delivery is personal or by first class mail. After 14 days without payment or departure, or the longer period some local governments set, the landlord can file.

The first hearing falls seven to 14 days after the summons issues. A landlord victory leads to judgment and a writ of recovery of the premises. Under Minn. Stat. 504B.345, the court generally stays that writ for a reasonable period not to exceed seven days, except in actions based on certain serious conduct or when a default judgment was entered. A winning tenant also gets costs and sealed court records.

Grounds for eviction, listed in Minn. Stat. 504B.285, include a holdover after the lease term ends, after rent becomes due under the lease terms, or after notice ending a tenancy at will. A landlord cannot bring an eviction solely because the tenant was a victim of violence or after the tenant ended the lease under Minn. Stat. 504B.206.

What special situations change the rules for a rented home?

A few circumstances change the usual periods. After a tenant dies, the landlord or the tenant's personal representative can end a fixed lease with two months of written notice taking effect on a month's last day, and the estate stays liable for rent before and during that time.

  • Tenants who fear imminent violence after domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion or harassment may end a lease with signed written notice and a qualifying document, and the landlord must keep the information private or face $2,000 in statutory damages plus fees.
  • A tenant whose lease began during a mortgage redemption period may be entitled to 90 days written notice from the successor after foreclosure, and landlords who learn of a foreclosure sale may only sign short leases under Minn. Stat. 504B.151.
  • To enforce an automatic renewal clause, the landlord must send a written reminder 15 to 30 days before the tenant's notice deadline.

Owners who prefer not to juggle showings, tenants and deposits can request an as-is cash offer on a Minnesota rental and write the deposit handling into the purchase agreement.

More questions about Minnesota Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

What happens to my security deposit if my Minnesota landlord sells the building?

The landlord must either transfer the deposit with interest to the buyer and notify you, or return it to you, within 60 days of the sale or when the buyer must account to you, whichever comes first. The buyer then holds the landlord's duties for it, and you have 20 days from the written notice to object to the stated amount.

Can my Minnesota landlord show my home to buyers without asking me?

Only after a good faith effort to give at least 24 hours of reasonable notice, naming a time or window between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless you agree to something else. Emergency entry is allowed without notice when the landlord reasonably suspects an immediate danger to people or property.

How long does a Minnesota landlord have to return a deposit?

Three weeks after the tenancy ends, or five days after a legal condemnation you did not cause, once the landlord has your mailing address. The landlord must return the deposit with interest or send a written statement of the specific reasons for any deduction.

How much notice does a Minnesota landlord give before filing an eviction for unpaid rent?

A written notice with the amount due and an itemized accounting, and then 14 days, or a longer local period if the city or county requires one. If you pay the full amount or move out in that time, the landlord cannot file on that notice.

Can a Minnesota landlord evict me for complaining about repairs?

No. Punishing a complaint with eviction, higher obligations or reduced services is barred. Within 90 days of the complaint the landlord has to prove it was not retaliation, and after that the tenant carries the burden.

title: Minnesota Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Minnesota Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Minnesota Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Minnesota Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Minnesota Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Minnesota House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Before an eviction for nonpayment, landlord must give written notice (total due, accounting, required statements) stating the tenant may be sued if not paid or moved out within 14 days; local rules may require longer. (Minn. Stat. 504B.321 subd. 1a; source)
  • The nonpayment notice must be delivered personally or by first class mail to the tenant at the leased premises. (Minn. Stat. 504B.321 subd. 1a(b); source)
  • An eviction action starts by filing a complaint with the court, with a copy of the written notice attached. (Minn. Stat. 504B.321 subd. 1; source)
  • Eviction lies when a tenant holds over after lease term expires or contrary to lease conditions, or a tenant at will holds over after notice to quit. (Minn. Stat. 504B.285 subd. 1(a)(2)-(3); source)
Selling in Minnesota?
We buy Minnesota houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What written notice comes before a Minnesota eviction for unpaid rent?

A landlord must give a written notice that lets the tenant cure the debt for 14 days before filing an eviction for unpaid rent or other money owed under the lease. Some local governments require a longer period, and the longer local period controls. The rule is Minn. Stat. 504B.321, subd. 1a.

The notice has to contain specific items, and a court dismisses the later case without prejudice, and expunges the file, if the landlord fails to attach a required notice to the complaint.

  • The total amount due, with an accounting that separates unpaid rent, late fees, and other charges.
  • The name and address of the person authorized to receive rent and fees for the landlord.
  • A statement that the tenant may seek legal help, with a pointer to Legal Aid and LawHelpMN.org.
  • A statement on applying for financial help through the county or Tribal social services office, MNBenefits.mn.gov, or the United Way line at 2-1-1 or 800-543-7709.
  • A statement that the landlord can file a case if the tenant neither pays nor moves out within 14 days of the notice date.

The landlord or an agent must deliver the notice personally or by first class mail to the tenant at the rental address. When a county agency receives a copy, it treats the notice as verification of the emergency for rental assistance and may not ask the tenant for more proof.

Once the 14 days pass with no payment and no move-out, the landlord may file the complaint. The court's summons then repeats the legal help and financial help statements, names how to join the hearing by phone or computer when that is offered, and states that the complaint is attached and filed.

How much notice does a month-to-month tenant get in Minnesota?

A tenancy at will ends with written notice at least as long as the gap between rent due dates or three months, whichever is shorter. A tenant who pays monthly is therefore entitled to one month, and a tenant who pays weekly is entitled to one week. Minn. Stat. 504B.135 lets either side end the tenancy this way.

When a tenant stays after the lease term ends, section 504B.141 says no tenancy longer than the shortest rent interval of the expired lease is implied for urban property unless the landlord expressly agrees. Holding over after a lease ends, or after a notice to quit, is itself a ground for eviction under section 504B.285.

Two statutes cover fixed leases that renew themselves or carry different notice periods:

  • A landlord who wants to enforce an automatic renewal in a lease of two months or longer must send a written reminder, personally or by certified mail, 15 to 30 days before the tenant's deadline to give notice (504B.145).
  • A landlord's notice to quit or notice of a rent increase may not be shorter than the notice period the lease gives the tenant, and the tenant may choose either period when leaving (504B.147).

Which Minnesota notices are longer, shorter, or skipped?

The table lists the notice periods most likely to affect a house that is rented, foreclosed, or inherited. Each row has its own statute, so check which one fits the tenant's situation.

Common eviction and lease-ending notice periods in Minnesota
SituationNotice or timingStatute
Unpaid rent14 days, or longer if local law says so504B.321, subd. 1a
Tenancy at willRent interval or three months, whichever is less504B.135
Tenant in a foreclosed home, lease began after the mortgageAt least 90 days after redemption ends504B.285, subd. 1a
Tenant in a home cancelled under a contract for deedAt least two months504B.285, subd. 1b
Federally subsidized housing losing its subsidyOne year504B.255
Lease ended by the death of a tenantTwo months, effective on the last day of a month504B.265
Unlawful activity covenant breachedNo set notice period, right to possession voided504B.171

Source: Minnesota Statutes chapter 504B. The death-of-tenant notice can come from the landlord or from the tenant's personal representative, and it does not erase rent or restoration costs owed to that point.

Does a breach or a retaliation claim change a Minnesota notice?

A breach of the lease covenant against unlawful activity under section 504B.171 voids the tenant's right to possession, though rent and the other lease terms stay in force until the lease ends. A landlord who alleges this breach, or conduct that seriously endangers other residents, can seek an expedited hearing with an affidavit of specific facts.

Notice to quit can also be answered by a retaliation defense. A tenant who proves by a fair preponderance of the evidence that the notice was meant as a penalty for a good faith effort to enforce rights, or for reporting a code violation, defeats the case. If the notice was served within 90 days of the tenant's protected act, the landlord carries the burden of showing it was not retaliatory (504B.285, subd. 2).

Landlords who ask tenants to pay through a digital platform must offer another way to pay when the platform is down, with no fee. A landlord who starts an eviction or charges late fees after both options failed faces dismissal and the tenant's attorney fees, according to the Judicial Branch landlord FAQ.

What do these notice rules mean for someone selling a Minnesota house with tenants?

They set how long a tenant can stay and what paperwork must exist before anything is filed. A seller who wants a tenant out before closing should serve the correct notice first, because a missing or defective notice leads to dismissal and an expunged case.

  • If the owner has received notice of a mortgage foreclosure sale, any new residential lease can run only two months or the time left in the redemption period, whichever is less, and the tenant must be told in writing before signing. The civil penalty for skipping the written notice is $500 (504B.151).
  • The mortgagor's redemption period after the sheriff's sale is six months for most homes, with a 12-month period in listed cases such as land over 40 acres (580.23).
  • A tenant's deposit passes to the buyer with interest, or goes back to the tenant, within 60 days of the sale (504B.178). Ask the county recorder and your closing agent what the title company needs to see about leases and recorded judgments.

Forms for starting a case are on the Judicial Branch's landlord forms page, which also offers Minnesota Guide and File.

More questions about Minnesota Eviction Notice Rules

How many days notice does a Minnesota landlord have to give to evict for nonpayment?

Fourteen days from the notice date, unless a local rule sets a longer period. The notice must be delivered personally or by first class mail to the rental address and must list the amount due, an accounting, and the required legal help and financial help statements.

Can a Minnesota landlord evict without any written notice?

For unpaid rent, no. The complaint must have the written notice attached, or the court dismisses the case without prejudice and expunges the file. Holdover and lease breach cases have different rules, and a case under section 504B.171 can be expedited.

How much notice must a landlord give to end a month-to-month tenancy in Minnesota?

Written notice at least as long as the rent period or three months, whichever is shorter. For a tenant paying monthly that is one month. The tenant gets the same notice rule when leaving.

What notice does a tenant get when the house is foreclosed?

At least 90 days' written notice to vacate, given no sooner than the end of the redemption period, for a tenant whose lease began after the mortgage was signed. A bona fide lease with more than 90 days left can run to its end, unless the new owner will live there.

Does a tenant's death end a Minnesota lease?

Yes, either side can end it on at least two months' written notice effective on the last day of a calendar month. The landlord or the estate's personal representative can send it. The estate still owes rent and restoration costs up to that point.
